title: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Extinction caused by Natural Selection”. Scope: species in fully occupied areas, over ecological and geological time

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rarity before extinction is directly testable with extensive current and fossil data. Demonstrating that favoured forms caused the decline, rather than merely covaried with it, remains difficult.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In ecological and fossil time series, test whether increases of putatively favoured competitors predict declines of others and whether declining occupancy or abundance precedes last appearance. Consistent competitor-linked decline and pre-extinction rarity support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shared environmental forcing can produce reciprocal abundance trends without competition.

Sampling decline creates apparent rarity before last fossil occurrence.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.58
data adequacy: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.82
analysis feasibility: 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rarity before extinction is a direct fossil-occurrence question, and public occurrence databases make the analysis a standard weeks-scale project for well-sampled groups. Sampling bias is severe enough that an apparent decline is not decisive, and the ecological zero-sum clause is only weakly tied to those geological counts. The data resolve a biased subset of the pattern rather than the competitive mechanism across fully stocked regions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In fossil occurrences, test whether occupancy declines in the intervals before last appearance beyond a sampling model, and in modern assemblages test whether increases in one species are matched by decreases in others. Pre-extinction rarity and negative abundance coupling would confirm the two clauses; extinctions that are as often preceded by high abundance, once sampling bias is removed, would refute the geological clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ecological time series are short relative to extinction.

The Signor-Lipps effect makes taxa look rare before their true last occurrence.

Calling the increasing form the favoured one uses the outcome the explanation is meant to predict.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.82
data adequacy: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.74
operationalizability: 0.74
